Dashboard Inheritance

**Why is this needed**:

I work in a team managing observability for thousands of instrumented applications.
I've made a general dashboard that shows a lot of useful information and has a variable+dropdown for the app name. In theory, this should be very simple to navigate, but we've got a ton of users who are brand new to observability, and we've found that it's sometimes a challenge to get them to

1. Locate this dashboard
1. Locate the dropdown
1. Select the app name

Ideally, I would like to give brand new users who know nothing about Grafana the ability to
1. Naively search for the app name in the global search bar
1. Click the `<app_name> Monitoring` result

If I want to do this right now, my only option seems to be to write some code to copy the contents of this general dashboard and make a brand new dashboard specifically for this app name, but that would quickly result in an explosion of disk space usage just for these service-specific dashboards.

**What would you like to be added**:

We could achieve the above goal while keeping disk space usage minimal if there were something like dashboard inheritance/virtualization/symlink/insert_sexy_tech_term_here. By this I mean:
* one parent dashboard (e.g., `App Monitoring Template`)
   * has everything that a normal dashboard has, e.g.,
      * rows
      * visualizations
      * data links,
      * dropdowns for non-hidden variables (e.g., SLO values like 95th percentile latency)
      * etc.
* hundreds to thousands of child dashboards whose json essentially looks like
```
{
    "type": "inherited",
    "name": "Foo Monitoring",          # name of new child dashboard
    "base": "App Monitoring Template", # name of template dashboard
    "values": {                        # values used to fill in the hidden variables in the template dashboard
        "app_name": "Foo"
    }
}
```

NB: I've taken a look at [this issue](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/issues/5657) and [this one](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/issues/1803) as well, but they don't seem to cover what I'm looking for. I'm not talking about reusable panels, I'm talking about adding a feature such that when I go to create a new dashboard, I am presented with a 4th option.

[image]

In this 4th option, I could select one of the available template dashboards and specify what variables I want to fill in with which values.
This would then create a new entry in the set of dashboards that looks like the above JSON.

Just spit-balling here, but the access/rendering algorithm could look like this:
1. Frontend:
   1. User clicks on the link to an inherited dashboard
1. Backend:
   1. Receives request
   1. Retrieves the JSON for the requested dashboard
   1. Notes that this is an `inherited` dashboard
   1. Pulls up record for the `base` dashboard
   1. Fills in in the variables and then proceeds with rendering process as though this were any other dashboard
   1. Sends the result to the frontend
1. Frontend does its stuff
1. User is presented with this parent+child renderingAs a concrete example, I currently have a default dashboard that I'm working on that looks like this:

[image]

If the user follows the three steps in the **Why is this needed** section, they can see telemetry about their app.

What I would prefer, though, is that rather than having the dropdown in the top left where the user needs to select their app name, I would turn this into a template dashboard where the app name is a hidden variable. I would then set up a CICD pipeline that would

1. turn this into a template dashboard with a hidden variable for `service_name`
1. set up a CICD pipeline to run once every hour, which would
   1. query the values for the `service` or `service_name` label in some metric (e.g., traces_spanmetrics_calls_total)
   1. for each service name in the results:
      1. check if this already has a child dashboard
      1. if no child dashboard exists: add a new child dashboard with "name": "<service> Monitoring" and "app_name": <service>"

Assuming an app name of `ASM_Service`, the result would be that within 1 hour of this app owner sending their `ASM_Service` traces to Tempo, they would automatically have an `ASM_Service Monitoring` dashboard that looks like so

[image]

That is, a dashboard which is fundamentally the same as the choose-your-own-app-name dashboard but for the small difference that we've done the work of filling in the app name variable for you and have given the dash a sane and easily-searchable name.

**Who is this feature for?**

This is for two people:
1. The engineers trying to make observability that "just works" such that we can maximize user adoption and utility while keeping resource usage to a minimum
1. App owners who are new to observability and who would like a way to easily navigate to a screen that lets them monitor their apps.

Dashboard API: OpenAPI schemas for CUE union types do not match the JSON wire format

The published OpenAPI for `dashboard.grafana.app` describes every CUE union of `*Kind` types as an object with one optional property per member. On the wire, a union is the member object itself, picked by its `kind` field. A client generated from the OpenAPI builds bodies the server cannot read.

Example, a Variable at v2:

| | Body |
|---|---|
| OpenAPI says | `{"spec": {"QueryVariableKind": {"kind": "QueryVariable", "spec": {...}}}}` |
| Server reads | `{"spec": {"kind": "QueryVariable", "spec": {...}}}` |

Sent in the OpenAPI shape, the union's `UnmarshalJSON` finds no top-level `kind` and leaves the union empty without an error ([dashboard_spec_gen.go L3452-L3455](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/a032971c4d16af2a657761e6f026595d93da0c8e/apps/dashboard/pkg/apis/dashboard/v2/dashboard_spec_gen.go#L3452-L3455)). For a Variable, validation then rejects it with `variable spec must include exactly one variable kind` ([variable.go L133](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/a032971c4d16af2a657761e6f026595d93da0c8e/pkg/registry/apis/dashboard/variable.go#L133)).

From the snapshots in `pkg/tests/apis/openapi_snapshots/`. No other API group's snapshot has this shape.

| Union | v2alpha1 | v2beta1 | v2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `VariableSpec` (Variable kind) | | yes | yes |
| `DashboardQueryVariableKindOr...SwitchVariableKind` (dashboard variables) | yes | yes | yes |
| `DashboardPanelKindOrLibraryPanelKind` (elements) | yes | yes | yes |
| `DashboardGridLayoutKindOrAutoGridLayoutKindOrTabsLayoutKindOrRowsLayoutKind` and `DashboardGridLayoutKindOrRowsLayoutKindOrAutoGridLayoutKindOrTabsLayoutKind` (layouts) | yes | yes | yes |
| `DashboardAutoGridLayoutKindOrGridLayoutKind` | | | yes |
| `DashboardConditionalRenderingVariableKindOr...TimeRangeSizeKind` | yes | yes | yes |
| `NotebookCellKindOrV2PanelKindOrLibraryPanelKind` and `NotebookMarkdownCellContentKindOrCodeCellContentKind` (notebooks) | | yes | |

The App SDK generates each CUE disjunction as a Go struct with one pointer per member and custom `MarshalJSON`/`UnmarshalJSON`. openapi-gen builds the schema from the struct fields and does not see the custom JSON methods ([zz_generated.openapi.go L5772](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/a032971c4d16af2a657761e6f026595d93da0c8e/apps/dashboard/pkg/apis/dashboard/v2/zz_generated.openapi.go#L5772)). Each member's `kind` is also published as a free string with default `""`. The CUE-derived manifest schema is already right: `"VariableKind":{"oneOf":[...]}` in [dashboard_manifest.go L38](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/a032971c4d16af2a657761e6f026595d93da0c8e/apps/dashboard/pkg/apis/dashboard_manifest.go#L38).

The frontend works around it by casting the generated client types to the CUE-generated ones, for example in [notebookResource.ts L70-L71](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/a032971c4d16af2a657761e6f026595d93da0c8e/public/app/features/notebook/api/notebookResource.ts#L70-L71). Clients generated straight from the OpenAPI have no such workaround.

1. **In the App SDK generator (preferred):** emit a schema for union types, a `oneOf` over the members with each member's `kind` pinned by an `enum`. openapi-gen uses a type's own `OpenAPIDefinition()` method instead of its fields when one exists, as [`ErrorDetails`](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/a032971c4d16af2a657761e6f026595d93da0c8e/apps/provisioning/pkg/apis/provisioning/v0alpha1/types.go#L1054-L1055) does. This fixes every version and app at once. Use the `enum` rather than a `discriminator`: kube-openapi's `spec.Schema` only has the OpenAPI 2 string form.
2. **Stopgap in this repo:** rewrite the affected schemas in the dashboard builder's [`PostProcessOpenAPI`](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/a032971c4d16af2a657761e6f026595d93da0c8e/pkg/registry/apis/dashboard/register.go#L1604-L1665), which already patches the v0alpha1 search schemas.
3. **Regression test:** validate real bodies from the dashboard and variable integration fixtures against the published snapshots with kin-openapi (already in `go.mod`).

Alerting: deleting a rule with a long version history times out on PostgreSQL (latest-version lookup scans every version)

**What went wrong?**

We hit this in production. Deleting an alert rule through the provisioning API (`DELETE /api/v1/provisioning/alert-rules/:uid`) took more than 30 s on our PostgreSQL backend, and the rule never got deleted.

For scale: one Grafana 13.2.0 instance on PostgreSQL 15 (RDS) with ~15k alert rules. The rules are managed through Terraform/Crossplane and re-applied often, and `rule_version_record_limit` was left at the default (unlimited), so each rule had built up ~130k stored versions.

We have `alertRuleRestore` on with the default `deleted_rule_retention`, so before deleting, `DeleteAlertRulesByUID` looks up the latest version of the rule to keep as the restorable copy. On `main` this no longer depends on the flag (since #135027). It runs whenever `deleted_rule_retention > 0`, and the default is `30d`, so every PostgreSQL instance on default settings runs this lookup on each rule delete:

```
SELECT v1.* FROM alert_rule_version AS v1
INNER JOIN (
    SELECT rule_guid, MAX(id) AS id
    FROM alert_rule_version
    WHERE rule_org_id = $1 AND rule_uid IN ($2)
    GROUP BY rule_guid
) AS v2 ON v1.rule_guid = v2.rule_guid AND v1.id = v2.id
```

That query is the slow part. `id` is only in the primary key, so to get `MAX(id)` Postgres has to visit every row of the rule's history in the table itself. Our rules are managed by Terraform/Crossplane and get rewritten a lot, and `rule_version_record_limit` defaults to 0 (keep everything), so each rule had around 130k versions. Performance Insights showed ~25 s and ~78k blocks read per call for one rule UID.

The client gives up at 30 s, the transaction rolls back, and it retries. So the delete never finishes, and the database keeps running these scans back to back. On our production RDS instance, read IOPS went from ~200/s to 6-17k/s and stayed there for about a day, until we paused the client. That load was shared with everything else Grafana does on the same database.

Grafana logged this at the same time:

```
logger=ngalert level=error msg="Failed to get latest version of deleted alert rules. The recovery will not be possible" error="pq: canceling statement due to user request (57014)"
```

**What did you expect to happen?**

Finding the latest version shouldn't require reading every old version of the rule from the table.

**Possible fix**

Use `MAX(version)` and join on `(rule_guid, version)`. Both are already covered by unique indexes, `(rule_org_id, rule_uid, rule_guid, version)` and `(rule_guid, version)`, so Postgres can do an index-only scan and skip the table. `version` is unique per GUID and goes up on every write, so it picks the same row `MAX(id)` does. MySQL and SQLite shouldn't see a difference, since their secondary indexes already carry the primary key.

I tried this locally on PostgreSQL 17.4 with the migrated schema. The table had 540k rows (422 MB), and the test rule had 130k versions mixed in with a few other busy rules:

```
                          plan                               buffers    time
MAX(id)                   parallel seq scan, whole table     ~54,000    37-229 ms
MAX(id), seqscan off      index scan + table fetch per row   ~53,700    186-383 ms
MAX(version)              index-only scan, 0 heap fetches      1,678    13-26 ms
```

Everything was cached locally, so the times are small. The buffer counts are the real difference (about 32x fewer). On RDS those were disk reads. I can send a PR.

**Workaround**

Setting `rule_version_record_limit` makes Grafana trim each rule's history the next time the rule is updated, and that avoids this. I don't think it should be needed, though. The default is unlimited, so any instance on default settings with frequently re-applied rules will hit this eventually. The limit also throws away the version history the rule history and restore features rely on. The fix above returns the same row from indexes that already exist, so it doesn't depend on how much history is kept.

**Related**

`CleanUpDeletedAlertRules` (`DELETE FROM alert_rule_version WHERE rule_uid='' AND created <= ?`) also scans the whole table on Postgres, because no index starts with `rule_uid`. We saw ~300k blocks and ~345 s per run. That one probably needs a new index, so I'd keep it separate.

**Environment**

Grafana 13.2.0, PostgreSQL 15 (RDS), ~15k alert rules, `alertRuleRestore` on, `rule_version_record_limit` = 0. The query is the same on `main`, where it also runs without the flag.

Git Sync: A bare y key in a YAML dashboard file is read as true

We keep our dashboards as YAML files (`apiVersion: dashboard.grafana.app/v1`, `kind: Dashboard`) in a repository Git Sync syncs. Every bare `y:` key in a panel's `gridPos` reaches Grafana as a `"true"` key, so no panel keeps its `y` and the panels stack on top of each other. A bare `refId: N` or `refId: Y` turns into the boolean `false` or `true` the same way.

Git Sync's own dry run shows it. The files endpoint returns a `gridPos` with a `"true"` key in place of `y`, in both `resource.file` and `resource.dryRun`. The saved dashboard JSON has the same key.

"gridPos": { "h": 1, "true": 0, "w": 24, "x": 0 }

`DecodeYAMLObject` in `pkg/registry/apis/provisioning/resources/fileformat.go` decodes the file with `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/serializer/yaml`, which runs on `sigs.k8s.io/yaml`. Dashboards: Dashboard preferences (org, folder and user tiers, plus "My view")

Today, settings such as `preload`, auto refresh, cursor sync and the default time range are baked into each dashboard's JSON. Every viewer gets the same value, and every new dashboard starts from hard-coded defaults.

This epic adds **dashboard preferences** in tiers. Each tier overrides the one above it:

| Tier | Applies to | Stored |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Org | dashboards created in the org | server (`namespace`) |
| Folder | dashboards created in the folder or its subfolders | server (`folder-<folderUID>`) |
| User | dashboards the user creates | server (`user-<userUID>`) |
| My view | one dashboard, for one user, in one browser | browser `localStorage` |

- **Org, folder and user preferences apply when a dashboard is created.** A new dashboard is seeded from the merged cascade. Existing dashboards never change when a preference changes.
- **"My view" is live.** It applies on load and is never saved. Saving writes the dashboard's stored values.

Phase 2 adds **panel preferences**, as groups that follow Grafana's shared visualization options: legend, tooltip and decimals. One Grafana-owned applier writes them into new built-in panels.

- Org and folder admins can't standardize how new dashboards behave.
- Viewers can't adapt a dashboard without changing it for everyone. For example, they can't turn on eager loading so in-page browser search works, or add a shared crosshair.
- `default_preload` in `grafana.ini` is the only setting today. It is instance-wide and applies only at creation.

- **Org admins:** preferences for the whole org.
- **Folder admins:** team preferences for a folder tree.
- **Every user:** personal preferences for dashboards they create, plus a per-dashboard "My view".

**Kind:** `DashboardPreferences` in `dashboard.grafana.app/v2beta1`, with one object per tier. The name alone identifies the tier: `namespace`, `folder-<folderUID>` or `user-<userUID>`.

**Fields.** Every field is optional, and an absent field inherits from the next tier. The spec has two sections:
- `spec.dashboard`: `preload`, `autoRefresh`, `autoRefreshIntervals`, `timeRange {from, to}` and `cursorSync`.
- `spec.panels`: `legend`, `tooltip` and `field.decimals`.

`spec.reset` lists fields that use Grafana's built-in default at this tier instead of inheriting from the next tier. A field can't be both set and reset in one tier.

Every string and list has a size limit.

**Endpoints:**

| Endpoint | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `GET / PUT / PATCH / DELETE …/dashboardpreferences/{name}` | Read or write one tier. PATCH creates a missing tier; `null` clears a field. |
| `GET …/dashboardpreferences` | Lists only the tiers the caller may read. |
| `GET …/dashboardpreferences/merged?folder=<uid>&includeUser=` | Resolves the creation cascade: user, then nearest folder, then parent folders, then org, then the built-in fallback. `sources` says which tier set or reset each field (D2). |

**Authorization:**

| Tier | Read | Write |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Org | members of that org | `orgs.preferences:write` (org admins by default) |
| Folder | folder viewers | folder admins (`folders.permissions:write`) |
| User | the owner | the owner |

- Anonymous and render identities get nothing.
- Git Sync can read and delete, but never write.
- Access-policy tokens can only delete, for folder and user cleanup.
- While the flag is off, Grafana's service identity can still get, list and delete, so cleanup keeps working.
- `merged` applies parent folders the caller can't read, without naming them (D1).
- A folder editor who is not a folder admin can manage folder variables, but not folder preferences.

**Not covered:**
- Import, templates, *Save as*, provisioning and API-created dashboards aren't seeded.
- Public dashboards, snapshots, and embedded, solo and render views don't get "My view" values.
- Library panels are pending D8.
- Time zone and week start stay with the existing Preferences: org, team and user.

- Everything is behind the `grafana.dashboardPreferences` feature flag (experimental, off by default).
- After the backend service deploys, keep the flag off for every tenant until folder cleanup, user cleanup and the multi-tenant folder app client are live. Otherwise, deletes leave orphaned preferences.
- Backend and frontend ship in separate PRs. Generated clients and schemas ship with the backend PR that changes them.

**M0 – UX**

**M1 – Backend service**

**M2 – "My view" (live, browser-only)**

**M3 – Server tiers in the UI**

**M4 – Phase 2: panel preferences**

**Critical paths:**

Alerting: nil pointer dereference in mail.v2 base64LineWriter when sending alert emails with file attachments (screenshots)

Grafana crashes repeatedly with a nil pointer dereference panic whenever alert email notifications are sent with file attachments (panel screenshots). Multiple goroutines panic simultaneously, causing the entire Grafana process to crash.

The panic originates in `gopkg.in/mail.v2@v2.3.1` at `writeto.go:299` inside `(*base64LineWriter).Write`, triggered by Grafana's `SmtpClient.setFiles` closure at `smtp.go:147` when base64-encoding a file attachment body.

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x18 pc=0x2c649c0]

goroutine XXXXX [running]:
gopkg.in/mail%2ev2.(*base64LineWriter).Write(...)
        gopkg.in/mail.v2@v2.3.1/writeto.go:299 +0xa0
encoding/base64.(*encoder).Write(...)
        encoding/base64/base64.go:253 +0x15b
github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/services/notifications.(*SmtpClient).setFiles.func1(...)
        github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/services/notifications/smtp.go:147 +0x30
[... 11 more lines]
```

This panic fires for **every alert email goroutine concurrently** — in the observed logs, 10+ simultaneous goroutines crash with identical stack traces.

The nil pointer dereference occurs at offset `0x18` of the `base64LineWriter` struct, which corresponds to its internal `w io.Writer` field. When `setFiles` constructs the attachment writer and passes it to `mail.v2`'s `writeBody`, the writer is either nil or becomes nil mid-write. The `mail.v2` library has no nil-guard at `writeto.go:299`, so it panics unconditionally.

This is related to a known upstream bug in the `gomail`/`mail.v2` library ([[go-gomail/gomail#89](https://github.com/go-gomail/gomail/issues/89)]), which describes an identical crash when embedding large files. The issue in that report was never fixed in the library itself.

**Option 1** — Disable screenshot capture entirely:
```
[unified_alerting.screenshots]
capture = false
```

**Option 2** — Use cloud storage upload instead of file attachment (avoids the `setFiles` path):
```
[unified_alerting.screenshots]
capture = true
upload_external_image_storage = true
```

Grafana should handle file attachment encoding errors gracefully without crashing. Specifically:

- If the `io.Writer` passed to the mail attachment closure is nil or becomes invalid during encoding, Grafana should catch the error, log a warning, and send the email without the attachment rather than panicking and taking down the entire process.
- Concurrent alert notification goroutines should be isolated from each other — a failure in one email send should not propagate and crash all other in-flight notification goroutines.
- At minimum, the panic should be recovered at the goroutine boundary (e.g. in `RetryStage` or `emailSender.SendEmail`) so the Grafana server process stays alive and other alerts continue to be processed normally.

Accessibility: Add action form input incorrectly labeled

Several Add action inputs are only visually labeled with placeholders, which are not good enough for labeling fields that aren’t immediately obvious. All of the “Key”, “Name”, and “Value” fields need visual labels added.

The read-only input with “Content-Type” as its value is serving as a label, and the input to be labeled by it is effectively not labeled at all.

The Headers (key and value) inputs could potentially be labeled as a group using a table for the section. Some extra care would need to be taken, and testing with a screen reader would be required to ensure it works clearly. Otherwise, this section needs to have visible labels for all inputs, and the inputs that are read only either need to have a label per that or could be converted into a definition list with explanation text.
